question.leadin: This emperor killed his mother Agrippina the Younger and his first wife Octavia and forced Seneca the Younger to commit suicide for his alleged involvement in the Pisonian Conspiracy.
question.text: Name this Roman emperor who was the first emperor to commit suicide, after learning that he had been sentenced to death in absentia.
question.answerHtml: Nero [accept Nero Claudius Caesar Augustus Germanicus, but do NOT accept Claudius, Caesar, Augustus, or Germanicus alone]
question.clue: This man's mother, Agrippina, dominated his decisions until he had her killed off.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about the real-life Roman namesakes of the Gamemakers from The Hunger Games.
swap.text: The Gamemaker Seneca Crane shares his name with Seneca the Younger, the tutor of this Roman Emperor. This man allegedly played a fiddle during the Great Fire of Rome.
swap.answerHtml: Nero Claudius Caesar Augustus Germanicus [accept Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus]
swap.clue: This man was advised by Anicetus to build a self-sinking boat to kill his mother Agrippina the Younger.

question.leadin: Bridges are often important military objectives, as they can create chokepoints to slow an army's advance or retreat.
question.text: In 312 CE, Constantine I soundly defeated Maxentius at the Battle of the Milvian Bridge, which spans this major river of Rome. Maxentius drowned in this river's waters during the battle.
question.clue: The first colonia was a city at the mouth of this river which imported grain and was named Ostia.

swap.leadin: The Lex Titia officially installed one of these groups in 43 BCE.
swap.text: Name these groups of three coequal Roman leaders, the second of which was comprised of Octavian, Marcus Lepidus, and Marc Antony.
swap.clue: One of these groups was given authority by the Lex Titia and fought the liberatores, and a member of another of these groups was assassinated immediately after arriving in Egypt.

question.leadin: The members of the First Triumvirate all had interesting deaths.
question.text: This man was stabbed on the floor of the Roman Senate by a team of rebellious senators. Following his victory in a civil war, this man convinced the Senate to declare him dictator for life, one month before his assassination.
question.clue: Outnumbered four to one, this man still achieved victory over Vercingetorix at the Battle of Alesia, conquering all of Gaul.

swap.text: In later Marxist historiography, this rebel leader of the third Servile war became a symbol of ancient class struggle. This former gladiator's troops were crucified en masse following their loss at the Battle of the Silarius River.
swap.clue: After Crassus defeated this man, Pompey arrived from Spain and took credit for the victory.

question.leadin: This man's wife drove over her dead father's body with a chariot in a road now known as the "Street of Crime."
question.text: Name this man who usurped Servius Tullius to become king of Rome. He himself was popularly overthrown after his son Sextus raped a woman named Lucretia.
question.answerHtml: Tarquin the Proud (or Lucius Tarquinius Superbus; prompt on Lucius Tarquinius)
question.clue: This last king of Rome was legendarily deposed and exiled after his son Sextus raped Lucretia, the wife of Lucius Collatinus.

swap.leadin: Answer some questions about historical events that appear in the worksof the Roman historian Tacitus.
swap.text: According to Tacitus, this ruler of the Iceni revolted against Roman rule after the death of Prasutagus. Suetonius Paulinus ultimately defeated this ruler near Paulerspury.
swap.clue: This person's popularity as a patriotic symbol in Victorian Britain was influenced by the theory that her name comes from a root meaning "victory" in Celtic.

question.leadin: Identify these regions subject to military incursions by Roman forces.
question.text: Decebalus's raids from this region prompted Domitian to launch the first of two namesake wars, whose second incarnation saw Trajan subjugate this region bounded by the Danube and the Carpathians. Its capital was at Sarmizegetusa.
question.clue: Soldiers of this region used the sickle-like falx during a war in which a bridge near the Iron Gates was built by Apollodorus.

swap.text: Androgynous priests known as Galli facilitated the worship of this Roman cult deity. Priests bathed in bull's blood to honor this mother goddess, whose cult became popular during the Second Punic War.

question.text: St Isidore aided in the conversion of Visigothic Spain to Catholicism. The Visigoths had earlier followed this doctrine, which asserted that the Son was subordinate to the Father, and which was condemned at the Council of Nicaea.
question.clue: The emperor Constantius espoused this belief, leading to its further condemnation at the First Council of Constantinople.

swap.leadin: During times of crisis, these people were often scapegoated and buried alive near the Colline Gate.
swap.text: Name these Roman priestesses who served 30-year terms maintaining the city's sacred fire.
swap.clue: According to Plutarch, these people were punished by being sealed in a chamber near the Colline Gate with only limited food and water.

question.leadin: Viriathus led a rebellion that Polybius called the "fiery war" in this region, where velites ("WAY-lee-tace") units failed to counter weapons like the pilum ("PEE-loom") and falcata in the Numantine War.
question.text: Identify this region that contained the mysterious Tartessos civilization. After Sulla's civil war, Quintus Sertorius led a revolt in this region, where "New Carthage" controlled rich silver mines before the Battle of Ilipa ("ILL-ipp-uh").
question.answerHtml: Hispania [accept Iberia or Iberian peninsula; accept Spain or España; accept Portugal; accept Catalonia or Catalunya; accept Hispania Baetica or Hispania Tarraconensis or Hispania Citerior or Hispania Ulterior; accept Lusitania or Lusitanian War; accept Andalusia or Andalucía; accept Murcia] (“New Carthage” is Cartagena.)
question.clue: Quintus Sertorius fought a namesake guerilla campaign in this region, which was finally conquered by Augustus in 19 BC. This home to the Cantabrians was originally divided into "Ulterior" and "Citerior" portions by the Romans.

swap.leadin: After the death of this woman's husband Prasutagus, she was flogged, her daughters were raped, and Rome annexed her husband's kingdom despite his will.
swap.text: Name this leader of the Iceni who led a namesake revolt against the Romans.
swap.clue: This ruler trounced the Ninth Legion but was defeated by Suetonius at the Battle of Watling Street.

question.leadin: Tarquin the Proud refused to buy these documents at first, leading 6 of them to be burnt.
question.text: Name these documents written in hexameter that were stored in the Temple of Jupiter Capitolinus and guarded by the Decemviri Sacris Faciundis. The general Flavius Stilicho supposedly ordered that they be destroyed.

swap.text: This wall and Hadrian's Wall were constructed by the Romans in Great Britain. Building of this wall began in 142 AD, with governor Quintus Lollius Urbicus supervising, and it ran from the Firth of Forth to the Firth of Clyde.
swap.clue: Arthur's O'on was built to be visible from here and Gildas is mistakenly said to have built it.

question.leadin: One part of this structure lends its name to the Vindolanda Tablets discovered in the 1970s.
question.text: Identify this structure whose archaeological remains can be found at sites like Brocolitia and Cilurnum.
question.clue: A birthday invitation was found on one of the Vindolanda tablets, which were unearthed near this structure.

swap.leadin: In 1916, right-wing art historian Giulio Giglioli discovered a group of statues from this civilization that included the Apollo of Veii.
swap.text: Name this ancient culture whose study was popular in Fascist Italy, when it was extolled as a pre-modern paragon of Italian heritage. The fasces symbol comes from this culture.
swap.clue: Priests of these people were the first to be called haruspices ("huh-RUSS-puh-sees") and made divinations from sheep entrails.

question.text: Curzio Inghirami botched his staged discoveries of Etruscan "scariths" by using paper instead of this material. The Zagreb Book is an Etruscan text written on this material that was found wrapped around an Egyptian mummy.
question.answerHtml: linen [or flax; accept Liber Linteus, Libri lintei, or linen rolls; prompt on textiles, fabric, or synonyms]

swap.leadin: Name the following people from early Roman history who may or may not have ever really existed, 5-10-20-30.
swap.text: This king of Clusium led an Etruscan army that attempted to restore the Tarquin monarchy and was eventually beaten by an alliance of Latin cities.
swap.clue: This figure was saved from death when a would-be assassin mistook his scribe for him, and that assassin thrust his right hand into a fire in an act of defiance against this figure.
